description: Postdoctoral research fellow at Victoria University of Wellington. Deep learning for mass spectrometry and chromatography, applied to seafood authentication and marine conservation.

tagline: I build deep learning models that read the chemical fingerprints of fish, to authenticate seafood and help protect the ocean it comes from.
about: I am a postdoctoral research fellow in the School of Engineering and Computer Science at Te Herenga Waka—Victoria University of Wellington, working with [Hiringa te Mahara](https://hiringatemahara.nz/), the Aotearoa New Zealand pod of [Abundant Intelligences](https://abundant-intelligences.net/), an Indigenous-led programme that reimagines AI from Indigenous knowledge systems. My postdoc is supervised by [Dr Kevin Shedlock](https://people.wgtn.ac.nz/kevin.shedlock). I collaborate with the [Bioeconomy Science Institute](https://www.bioeconomyscience.co.nz/), formerly Plant & Food Research, and sit on the board of the [AI Research Association of Aotearoa New Zealand](https://www.airesearchers.nz/) as the elected representative for postdoctoral researchers.

I hold a BE (Hons) in Software Engineering and a PhD in Artificial Intelligence. Before the PhD I was a software developer intern and later a contract software engineer at NIWA, New Zealand's National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research. I still think of code as a scientific instrument: something to build carefully, test and then point at an open question. Off the clock I built a Skyrim-style wellbeing tracker and am currently lost somewhere in Baldur's Gate 3.

intro: My research sits where machine learning meets analytical chemistry. A mass spectrometer or a gas chromatograph turns a piece of fish into a long vector of numbers, and the interesting question is what a model can learn from that signal: which species it is, which part of the fish, whether it has been adulterated and which batch it came from. Right now that means deep learning on GC-MS chromatograms to authenticate fish species, framed through kaitiakitanga and aimed at protecting marine resources from illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. My thesis did the same for rapid evaporative ionisation mass spectrometry, where transformers reached 100% accuracy on species identification and a self-supervised method, SpectroSim, traced samples to their batch without labels. I care most about self-supervised learning, transformer architectures and evaluation rigorous enough that a chemist would trust the result.
